title: What 25 Trillion Tokens Reveal About How Developers Actually Adopt AI Agents
gist: Kilo Code's Brendan O'Leary uses gateway data from over 40 trillion tokens to argue that AI agent adoption is gated by earned trust, not benchmarks. Heavy users overwhelmingly run models from multiple labs, and adoption breaks at context construction, model routing and feedback loops.

insights.claim: Developer adoption of AI coding tools climbs a four-rung trust ladder (autocomplete, chat, single agent, orchestrated multi-agent), and each rung requires more trust while providing slower, sparser feedback evidence.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Evaluate agent vendors and internal rollouts by which rung users actually reach, not by model capability claims.
insights.locator: The Adoption Ladder

insights.claim: Most engineering teams today sit between rungs 1 and 3 of the ladder, and AI projects that skip the crawl-walk-run progression of trust (jumping straight to agent swarms) are prone to fail before production.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Expect enterprise agent budgets to stall where governance and trust infrastructure is missing; favor vendors selling the trust layer.
insights.locator: Then, once you get used to that, you can move up

insights.claim: Capability narratives (benchmark scores, context window sizes) have little to do with whether developers adopt a model; some teams build real dependency on models that benchmark worse but work for their use case.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Do not read benchmark leadership as a proxy for usage share or revenue; check usage-based data such as gateway share.
insights.locator: Opening framing

insights.claim: Trust in AI agents is asymmetric: many positive experiences are needed to build it and one visible failure can destroy it, so a single high-profile agent failure in front of a skeptical senior engineer can set an organizational narrative that takes long to reverse.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Rollouts should start with patient early adopters and build social proof; blanket access invites reputational setbacks that slow enterprise adoption.
insights.locator: Trust Is Measurable

insights.claim: Kilo Code's gateway has processed over 40 trillion tokens and offers access to more than 500 models, with the data excluding anonymous users, internal users, autocomplete and automated traffic.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: The scale suggests the token-volume growth curve in coding has not saturated; discount for the sample's early-adopter skew.
insights.locator: The Dataset

insights.claim: Kilo Code's user base skews to early adopters seeking open-source configurable tooling, so its usage patterns are better read as a leading indicator of where mainstream adoption goes in 12-18 months than as an average.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Treat the multi-model and agent figures as directional signals, not market-wide measurements.
insights.locator: The Dataset

insights.claim: Coding is among the most prevalent token-consuming use cases, with Kilo Code having topped OpenRouter's token usage rankings for months.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Coding agents are a primary demand driver for inference; watch OpenRouter rankings for demand shifts.
insights.locator: OpenRouter is a router that publishes rankings

insights.claim: Context construction (which files are included, whether the codebase is indexed, how the problem is stated) is where most adoption friction occurs, and bad AI output is typically bad context rather than a bad model.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Retrieval and context tooling, not raw model quality, is where differentiation and value capture in coding agents may sit.
insights.locator: Three Failure Points

insights.claim: Developers stuck in heavy chat without moving to agents consume higher token counts per request because they paste context manually, which signals failed context construction.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Rising tokens per request can indicate friction rather than productive use; look at usage mix by rung.
insights.locator: I think this shows up in the usage data indirectly

insights.claim: A stale semantic index of a codebase can be worse than letting the agent explore on its own, since a slightly outdated map wastes time and erodes trust; retrieval should favor relevance over recency.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Index freshness is a product requirement for code-context vendors; stale indexing is a churn risk.
insights.locator: I also think that stale context is a real thing

themes.theme: Failure point: model routing and multi-lab usage

insights.claim: In April, 68% of Kilo developers manually selecting models used models from two or more AI labs in the same month, and 45% of those switched models within the same hour.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: The single-best-model deployment assumption is wrong for sophisticated users; model-agnostic tooling has an edge over lab-locked tooling.
insights.locator: In April, 68% of folks

insights.claim: Among enterprise developers on Kilo, 71% ran models from two or more labs, up significantly from the first quarter.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Enterprises are adopting multi-vendor model access, a headwind for any single-lab lock-in strategy.
insights.locator: Then among enterprise developers

insights.claim: Multi-lab usage rises with usage intensity: light users average 1.5 labs (34% multi-lab), regular users 2.9 (76%), heavy users 5.3 (89%), and power users over 10,000 requests a month average 7.6 labs (92%).
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Multi-model use is a learning curve, so as users mature expect more routing across labs and weaker per-lab loyalty.
insights.locator: light, regular, heavy, and power

insights.claim: The model market is diversifying rather than consolidating: the top 10 models by request volume came from six labs, MiniMax-M2 Pro was the most requested model on some days, and no model exceeded 37% of requests on any day.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Open-weight and challenger labs can win meaningful coding share, pressuring frontier labs' pricing power.
insights.locator: The top 10 models in our dataset

insights.claim: Anthropic's share of Kilo gateway requests fell from 11.2% to 6.5% in the eight weeks through April even as total users and request volume grew 3x, reflecting diversification rather than a loser.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Frontier labs' relative share in open gateways is declining even as absolute usage grows; monitor share, not just volume.
insights.locator: Anthropic's share of our gateway requests dropped

insights.claim: Of developers who frequently switch models, 38% switch between free and paid models and 33% compare two paid models, with free models often being fresh releases, stealth models or subsidized offerings.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Free and stealth-model distribution is a customer-acquisition channel for labs and shows price sensitivity in model choice.
insights.locator: Thirty-eight percent of those that do switch models

insights.claim: Enterprises are using multiple model providers partly for business continuity, worried about lab policy changes, infighting and acquisition or consolidation, and single-provider teams worry about this concentration risk more.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Provider concentration risk is a purchasing criterion; multi-provider gateways and routers benefit.
insights.locator: business continuity dimension

themes.theme: Failure point: feedback loops and measuring trust

insights.claim: Many developers stay at the chat rung not because agents failed but because, when something went wrong, they lacked the signal to understand why, so the more useful diagnostic for failed agent projects is whether the feedback loop was right, not what the agent did wrong.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Observability and reasoning-trace tooling for agents is a gating product category for scaling autonomy.
insights.locator: Three Failure Points, third failure point

insights.claim: Agent tooling must surface what the agent decided and what context it had, not only what it did, otherwise developers watch briefly, lose confidence, and stop or take over the work themselves.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Favor agent products with intermediate signals and transparent reasoning; these are likely to retain users at higher autonomy levels.
insights.locator: Your tooling has to surface what agents decided

insights.claim: Trust can be proxied per rung: autocomplete override rate, chat session depth and follow-up rate, and agent session completion versus interruption rate.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: These are usable KPIs for diligence on AI dev-tool adoption beyond seat counts or token volume.
insights.locator: Trust Is Measurable

insights.claim: Adoption should be tracked as a continuum, for example how many users of autocomplete in 30 days moved to chat and then to multi-agent orchestration, rather than as a token leaderboard.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Ask AI tool companies for rung-migration retention, not just token volume, as a quality-of-growth metric.
insights.locator: Do developers move up that ladder?

insights.claim: AI tooling should treat context as infrastructure rather than a feature, be designed for provider independence from the start, and match the feedback loop to the adoption rung; assuming a single model pushes sophisticated users to route around the tooling.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Closed single-model developer tools risk losing power users; model-agnostic harnesses are structurally favored.
insights.locator: treating context as infrastructure, not as a feature

insights.claim: Tool-calling competence is now table stakes across frontier and large open-weight models, so agent harnesses differentiate less on agentic capability and more on the surface where they meet the user and on freedom to try multiple models.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Commoditization of tool calling narrows the moat of harness vendors; distribution and UX matter more.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers, harness question

insights.claim: The most senior engineers, who have deep systems understanding, get the most value from coding agents because they know how to supply the right context and can trust agents with well-scoped work.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: AI coding productivity may accrue most to experienced engineers, affecting hiring and team-composition assumptions.
insights.locator: some of the most senior engineers

insights.claim: Models have become good at reviewing code for intent, and a local review agent run at the end of a turn is now used almost every time by the speaker.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: AI-based review is becoming a default workflow step, a likely area of tooling spend.
insights.locator: we added a local review agent at the end of a turn

insights.claim: The same open-weight model served by different inference providers on OpenRouter can perform differently due to implementation and caching differences, so the gateway builds filtering to deliver the expected behavior.
insights.speaker: Brendan O'Leary
insights.so_what: Inference-provider quality variance is a hidden risk and a differentiator for routing and gateway layers.
insights.locator: OpenRouter which is one of the backends that we use
